title: System Services
summary: System Services covers execution that goes through the operating system's service or daemon manager rather than a user starting a program directly. On Windows this is the Service Control Manager, reachable through the graphical services console, sc.exe, PowerShell service cmdlets, Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) and remote procedure calls; on macOS and Linux the equivalents are launchd and systemd. An adversary favours a service because it runs without an interactive logon, inherits the rights of its service account, and appears in logs as ordinary administrative work. Execution may be one-off, where a service is created, started and deleted within seconds, or it may double as persistence. Artefacts include service creation records, service control manager operational events, registry changes under the services key, process creation for sc.exe or net.exe with service arguments, and short lived services whose binary appears and disappears. Defenders separate this from legitimate activity by tracking which accounts and hosts normally install services, requiring change records for new service binaries, and flagging service image paths outside standard program directories.

beginner.definition: A service is a program that runs in the background without anyone logging in. This technique is about attackers using the service system to start their own code. They may create a new service or change an existing one. The service system is powerful, so their code can run with high rights.
beginner.whyItMatters: Services start automatically and often run as a privileged account, which is exactly what an attacker wants. Administrators create and change services all the time, so the activity can look perfectly normal. If you do not record who installs services and which files they point to, malicious code can run for months. Services are also a common way to move from one computer to many.
howItWorks: The attacker gains the right to create or change a service, usually through an administrator level account.
They point a new or existing service at a program of their choice, including its full file path.
They start the service, and the service manager launches that program with the service account rights.
The program may run once and be removed, or stay installed so that it starts again after a reboot.
Remote versions of the same tools let one machine start a service on another machine across the network.
Defenders look for new service records, unusual file paths, and services that exist only briefly.
beginner.example: Think of a hotel with a maintenance panel that can switch the power in any room on or off. Staff use the panel every day, so seeing it used is normal. A thief who learns the panel code can start a machine in a locked room without ever entering it. The log shows a routine maintenance action. Abusing system services is like using that panel to run something in a room you cannot enter.
takeaways: Record which accounts and hosts are allowed to install services, and alert on everyone else.
A service whose program file sits in a temporary folder or user directory is a strong warning sign.
Some service abuse lasts only seconds, so collect process and service logs rather than assuming persistence.

objectives: Explain what a system service is and why attackers use the service manager for execution.
Describe how service creation differs from modifying an existing service.
Identify the process, service and registry artefacts this technique leaves behind.
Explain how remote service tools support movement between computers.
Describe how to distinguish legitimate administration from suspicious service activity.
